title: The USSR: SETKA and the Soviet programmes
notes: SETKA and the Soviet and Russian programmes.

lead.text: From 1978 to 1990 the Soviet Union ran a classified state programme on what it called anomalous phenomena, SETKA, split between the Ministry of Defence and the Academy of Sciences and run from Moscow; the programme's own published history says it found nothing extraterrestrial, while British defence intelligence judged the Soviet effort was probably about exploiting the phenomena.

summary.text: Accounts of the programme trace it to a surge of reports in 1977-1978, especially the Petrozavodsk phenomenon of 20 September 1977, which Izvestia reported as an unidentified natural phenomenon: a huge star with beams of light that hung over the town like a jellyfish.

The programme had two branches: SETKA-MO, led from a central military research institute in the Moscow region, and SETKA-AN, whose head institute was IZMIRAN under Academician V. Migulin, with a small working group headed by Yury Platov.

The main published account is the history co-written by Platov, who headed the academic working group, and B. Sokolov; the board carries its contents at Tier 2 and has obtained no Russian-language archival record of the founding documents.

As censorship lifted, a public Inter-Industry Ufology Research Centre with institute rights under the Academy of Sciences was set up in 1990, headed by Vladimir Azhazha; the board knows of it chiefly through a British intelligence report.

record.text: The UK's Project Condign, Volume 3, states that the Former Soviet Union clearly took the study of UAPs seriously and that this may well relate to a programme of understanding and exploiting UAP-related natural phenomena such as plasmas.
The same chapter summarises two Russian scientific papers in which 20-30 scientists appear to have researched the prevention of air target detection, followed by three redacted lines.

Condign records a UFO Commission created in 1989 under the USSR Union of Scientific and Engineering Societies and, in 1990, the inter-industry centre to coordinate records, with the rights of an Academy of Sciences institute, headed by V. G. Azhazha, a former naval submariner; its stated remit was ufology as a science of UFOs and their relation to the Earth's biotechnosphere.
IZMIRAN is the Pushkov Institute of Terrestrial Magnetism, Ionosphere and Radio Wave Propagation of the Russian Academy of Sciences, founded in 1939.
The programme was run from Moscow: the founding council of the Military-Industrial Commission met in the Kremlin in October 1977, and both the military executor and IZMIRAN were in the Moscow region.

claimed.text: According to Platov and Sokolov's history, the Academy's president asked the Military-Industrial Commission for an urgent research programme, the Commission's council noted that servicemen's reports sometimes involved disruption of military equipment, and two topics entered the 1978 defence plan: the military one on the phenomena's effect on equipment and personnel, the academic one on their physical nature.

The history says a General Staff directive of 1980 made the central military institute the collection centre and, for 13 years, put the army on watch for such phenomena across practically the whole USSR, every serviceman becoming without knowing it a potential participant; Navy guidelines were issued the same year.

It gives three reasons for secrecy: the work formally sat in the classified defence plan, a military-technical origin was thought likely at first, and some properties, such as the absence of radar contrast and high manoeuvrability, might have military use; official papers used the term paranormal phenomenon instead of UFO.

The history says the programme cost almost nothing, paid from the executing organisations' own budgets with no special financing, was renamed Galaktika in 1981 and Gorizont in 1986, and left a group analysing reports at the Academy until 1996.

Condign quotes a Sokolov describing 40 cases in which Soviet pilots encountered UFOs, were ordered to chase and then shoot, and lost control and crashed three times, twice fatally, after which pilots were told to observe and turn away.

One account of an Institute 22, created in 1978 by the Academy and the Ministry of Defence, says it investigated about 3,000 reports and left 5-10% unexplained; on the board's reading it is most likely the same apparatus as SETKA under another name.

Condign says Azhazha's institute reportedly developed filters and infrared and ultraviolet photography and obtained imagery of peculiar spheres and humanoid figures, adding that if the imagery exists it has never been published.

contested.text: Platov and Sokolov's history reports about 3,000 messages and over 400 events registered as extraordinary, more than 90% resolved as rocket launches or high-altitude balloons, and attributes Petrozavodsk itself to the launch of the Kosmos 955 satellite from Plesetsk.

The same history records no report of a landing, of contact with occupants, or of abduction in 13 years, and concludes that either the USSR was closed to alien visits or the extraterrestrial hypothesis fails.

The records point different ways: that history finds nothing anomalous, while critics quoted in another account allege the academic branch was a cover for a more serious military one, Condign judges the effort exploitation-driven, and the Sokolov quoted in Condign describes fatal pursuits.
The history itself leaves one series open: the 1984-87 flight emergencies at the Borisoglebsk air unit, with unknown objects on radar and seen by pilots, on which it says there is no consensus.

A 1977 preliminary report for the Academy concluded that the Petrozavodsk phenomenon could not be satisfactorily understood from the available data; northern European governments wrote asking whether it was Soviet weapons testing.

Condign names only Azhazha for the 1990 centre; the claim that the cosmonaut Pavel Popovich was its president rests on a secondary source, and the 1993 documents obtained by Knapp came from the Ministry of Defence via Colonel Boris Sokolov, not from the KGB file handed to Popovich. The board's link from the centre to SETKA is an inference with no document of transfer.
COMETA cites Soviet statistical studies as comparable to French ones, but on the board's reading this does not name SETKA or any Soviet body.

questions: Where are the Russian-language founding documents of SETKA, and do they match Platov and Sokolov's account?
Is the Sokolov quoted by Condign on fatal pursuits the same Sokolov who co-wrote a history finding no contact of any kind, and if so how are the two accounts reconciled?
Was the military branch more substantive than the academic one, as Stonehill and Mantle and Colonel Aleksandr Plaksin later argued?
Are Institute 22 and SETKA the same organisation?
What happened at Borisoglebsk between 1984 and 1987?
Did Azhazha's centre ever publish the imagery Condign says it reportedly obtained, and when did Azhazha die?
